title: Real Gases Are Expressed in Terms of Partial Fugacities
lead: A real gas does not follow the ideal chemical potential, so its pressure is replaced by a fugacity. How far the fugacity strays from the pressure follows from the gas's compression factor.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise is new and AI-written, with an AI solution checked by computation.

exercises.prompt: Up to moderate pressures a gas at fixed temperature follows $Z = 1 + B'p$ with $B' = -5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ bar−1. At $p = 50$ bar find (a) $\ln \gamma$, (b) the fugacity coefficient $\gamma$ and (c) the fugacity $f$.

answer.solution:
(a) $(Z - 1)/p = B'$, so $\ln \gamma = \int_0^{p} B'\,dp = B'p = (-5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{bar}^{-1})(50\ \text{bar}) = -0.25$.

(b) $\gamma = e^{-0.25} = 0.779$.

(c) $f = \gamma p = 0.779 \times 50\ \text{bar} = 38.9$ bar. With $Z$ below 1 the attractions dominate and the gas's fugacity is below its pressure.

derivations.what: the fugacity coefficient from the compression factor
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 26.10 Real Gases Are Expressed in Terms of Partial Fugacities

steps.cap: With $d\kT = 0$ the entropy term drops, and dividing by $d\kp$ gives the derivative at constant temperature.

nodes.note: The book prints the differential as $d\mu - Vdp - SdT$; it is $d\mu = V\,dp - S\,dT$.

steps.cap: Differentiate both sides with respect to pressure at constant temperature.
$\kmustd$ and $\kfstd$ do not depend on $\kp$, and $\ln(\kf/\kfstd) = \ln \kf - \ln \kfstd$.

nodes.note: The book differentiates "with respect to pressure at constant volume"; the derivative is taken at constant temperature, as its subscript $T$ says.

The book multiplies by $p/RT$ and writes $\left[\partial \ln f/\partial p\right]_T = pV/RT = Z$. Dividing by $RT$ gives $\left[\partial \ln f/\partial p\right]_T = V/RT = Z/p$; it is $p\left[\partial \ln f/\partial p\right]_T$ that equals $Z$.

assumes.text: Every gas behaves ideally as $\kp \rightarrow 0$, so there $\gamma = 1$ and $\ln\gamma = 0$.

steps.cap: The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.
Differentiate both sides with respect to $\kp$ at constant temperature.
Integrate from 0, where $\ln\gamma = 0$, up to the pressure $\kp$.

nodes.note: The book's middle line, $\int \left(\frac{Z}{\partial p} - \frac{1}{\partial p}\right)_T dp$, means $\int \left(\frac{Z}{p} - \frac{1}{p}\right)_T dp$.
